blocks.md:
1. **Supply and demand still rule.** In regressions of the college/high-school log wage gap, 1963–2005, the relative supply coefficient stays around −0.4 to −0.7 when the real minimum wage is added.
2. **The minimum wage adds little.** Its coefficient is small and imprecise (−0.049 to −0.144).
3. **Conclusions:** institutions "do not much alter the central role" of relative supply and trend demand, and are "insufficient to resolve the puzzle" of slowing trend relative demand for college workers after 1992.
Do "revisionist" explanations — institutions such as the falling minimum wage — rather than technology-driven demand account for rising US wage inequality?

March CPS, 1963–2005; the composition-adjusted college premium and relative supply as in the [Canonical Model of the Skill Premium](note:canonical-model-of-the-skill-premium); the real federal minimum wage (PCE-deflated) and the prime-age male unemployment rate.
OLS time-series regressions of the college premium on log relative supply, time trends (with a post-1992 break or polynomials), the log real minimum wage and unemployment.

blocks.md: The relative supply coefficient stays around −0.4 to −0.7 with the minimum wage included; the minimum's own coefficient is small and imprecise (−0.049 to −0.144). Trend demand growth still has to slow after 1992 to fit the data.
- 43 annual observations and the federal minimum only: little variation to identify the minimum's effect.

blocks.md: The macro view at the start of the lecture's last section: at the national level, the minimum wage seemed to matter little for the college premium. Vogel (2025) revisits both conclusions.
